notes.fact_check: 2026-09-27 GREEN with "about 425,000 cells from about 110 organoids"; tie "aged on schedule" to DNA-methylation clocks; "knows how old it is" only with "in effect". Nature, 19 Aug 2026, DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10877-x. Senior author Paola Arlotta, first author Irene Faravelli. Some organoids kept to about seven years.

caption:
Lab-grown cortical organoids kept alive for five years matured through fetal-, newborn- and early-childhood-like stages, and their DNA methylation clocks matched the time spent in the dish. About 425,000 cells profiled from about 110 organoids. Arlotta lab, Harvard and the Broad Institute. Nature, August 2026. The resemblance is in gene expression, not function.

Source on slide 8.

slides.title: This blob of brain has been alive for *5 years*
slides.sub: And by its DNA-methylation clock it knows, in effect, how old it is. Nature, August 2026.

slides.title: cortical organoids, still growing
slides.body: Lab-grown clusters of brain cells from the Arlotta lab at Harvard and the Broad Institute.

slides.title: Methylation clocks matched *dish time*
slides.body: Methylation clocks read chemical marks on DNA that track age. Here they lined up with how long each organoid had been growing.

slides.title: cells profiled
slides.body: From about 110 organoids, combining new and earlier data. Faravelli, Arlotta and colleagues.

slides.fact: They resemble brain tissue in gene expression, not in function
slides.body: The match is molecular. Function was not shown.

slides.title: The ethics question comes up *every time*
slides.body: As organoids get older and more lifelike, the debate about how to treat them grows with them.
